The problem

Specialty coffee is a retail business dressed as a craft one.

The industry's premium tier buys green beans it did not grow, applies heat it did not design, and sells the result as craft. The actual chemistry — what happens inside the cherry, before anyone lights a roaster — is left to chance.

Processing loses bioactives

Conventional processing and roasting degrade a substantial share of green-bean compounds — chlorogenic acids and trigonelline chief among them.

Premium without engineering

A café that sources a washed lot and roasts it well has added craft, not chemistry. The compound profile it sells is the one it received.

No one measures the cup

Specialty grading scores flavour. Almost nobody publishes a certificate of analysis for what is actually in the coffee.

The insight

Fermentation is not flavour decoration. It is molecular engineering.

Controlled fermentation changes which compounds survive into the cup and in what concentration. Treat it as a production variable rather than a regional tradition and coffee becomes something you can specify — the way a formulator specifies an ingredient.

The chain — four controlled stages

01

Bean selection

Lots chosen for bioactive potential, not flavour score alone.

Bioactive preservation

Low-temperature processing to hold molecular integrity.

Batch-level testing for compound content and purity.

At origin — Colombia

The launch line — four protocols

Four processes. Four different molecules.

Each protocol is a distinct production route with a distinct target. Two further protocols — lactic-acid and triple-washed — stay in pipeline until the launch four have batch data behind them.

Protocol 01

Anaerobic

Cherries ferment in fully sealed, oxygen-deprived tanks. Removing oxygen changes which microbes dominate and how far fermentation runs.

Target · chlorogenic acid retention

Protocol 02

Alcohol-infused

Spirits introduce additional fermentable sugars that feed native yeasts, extending fermentation and building aromatic depth.

Target · aromatic complexity

Protocol 03

Flavour-infused

Natural botanicals introduced under controlled infusion produce pronounced fruit and berry expression without added flavourings.

Target · sensory differentiation

Protocol 04

Ultrasound-assisted extraction

Cavitation ruptures cell walls mechanically rather than thermally, releasing compounds in 60 min where conventional extraction takes 12 hrs.

Target · extraction yield & speed

Evidenced today

Honey processing is already in commercial trade.

Beans carrying mucilage through the drying stage — the honey process. Colita ships Black Honey and Yellow Honey lots today under its own export marks. Differentiated processing is not a plan here; it is a running operation.

Sealed-vessel anaerobic fermentation is the step still to be documented — in photographs and in laboratory data.

One structural question this deck must answer

Ultrasound-assisted extraction is an extraction technology, not a bean-processing one. It either produces a concentrated compound extract we sell or license, or it accelerates a step inside bean production. Those are two different companies with two different cost structures. The answer belongs on this page before the raise opens.

UK market pricing — primary research, Aug 2026

Where fermented coffee actually sells in Britain.

Live retail pricing pulled from UK roasters, normalised to pounds per 100 g so formats compare. Two findings change how Colita should be positioned.

Alcohol-infused / barrel-aged Anaerobic fermented Rare & competition lots Colita implied price

Finding 1 — alcohol-infused is a novelty tier, not a premium one

Barrel-aged coffee sells below anaerobic in the UK. It reaches market through gift boxes, distillery collaborations and Great Taste Awards rather than specialty grading. Leading with alcohol-infused would anchor Colita to the cheapest of the four protocols.

Finding 2 — Colita's own pricing sits mid-commodity

The existing model — $1.50/cup at 50 cups/kg — implies roughly £5.90 per 100 g at current rates. That lands beside ordinary anaerobic lots and below Carter Coffee's Ethiopian. A coffee claiming laboratory verification cannot be priced like an unverified one.

The positioning consequence

The price ceiling is real. It is just not where the deck currently sits.

The gap between £5.90 and £43 is not a pricing decision. It is an evidence decision.

UK buyers already pay seven times the commodity-specialty price — but they pay it for varietal rarity and competition provenance, both of which are independently verifiable. Colita's claim is different in kind: not a rarer bean, but a measurably different one. That claim can command the same premium, and it can only be sold with a certificate of analysis behind it.

The numbers converge

  • Colita today £5.90 per 100 g sits beside the COE auction average of £5.34 — the price a merely-certified winner fetches
  • The £18–25 target band brackets the Colombia COE winning lot at £23.45 — near dead centre

Two independent routes — UK retail listings and public auction results — arrive at the same conclusion. The target band is what certification is worth, priced by the open market.

What 95–96 would mean, and what it needs

A 95–96 is above every Cup of Excellence winner on record. Recent COE champions top out at 92.32 (Brazil 2024) and 92.00 (El Salvador 2024). Only Best of Panama Geisha has passed 95, reaching 97 and 98 for the first time in 2025.

Producer-side scores routinely run several points above an international jury on the same lot. Presented uncertified, a 95–96 is the most falsifiable claim in this deck: the first question any specialty buyer asks is “scored by whom?”

Certified, it is transformational. A 90.61 earned £23.45 per 100 g. The route is a jury, not a louder claim.

One complication on the route

Colombia ran Cup of Excellence annually from 2005 to 2023 but is absent from the 2025 and 2026 COE calendars, having moved toward domestic auctions. The Colombian Association for Coffee Excellence (ASECC) is the body to approach; the alternative is a national or private auction with an independent certified jury.

Either way the requirement is identical to the laboratory work: an outside panel, a published score, a batch anyone can trace.

Converted at 453.59 g per pound and approximately $1.27/£1. What already exists

Sensory QC runs. Instrumental analysis does not.

Colita already cups systematically — dozens of samples to the table, coded and scored. That is a real quality system and most producers do not have one.

But cupping measures flavour. It cannot measure chlorogenic acid. The gap is not rigour — it is instrument. The same discipline pointed at an HPLC is what turns every Target chip above into a result.

The distinction that decides the raise

The 25 cited studies establish what chlorogenic acid and coffee polyphenols do. They do not establish what Colita's coffee contains. Blending those two on one slide is the exact move that destroyed green-coffee credibility a decade ago. One honest COA on one protocol against one control is worth more to this raise than all four percentage figures.

Not yet in the model

  • UK import duty and clearance on Colombian green coffee
  • Food business registration and ongoing compliance
  • Roasting or co-packing if not held in-house

An 80% gross margin on a $0.30 cup is a real starting point — but no investor underwrites gross margin. This table needs a contribution-margin column before the ask.

What the customer pays — cost per serving

At verified pricing, Colita stops being the cheap option — and that is the point.

Anyone wanting chlorogenic acid in their day has three routes. Priced as it is today, Colita undercuts all of them. Priced as the evidence would justify, it costs about the same as either — and replaces both.

Colita, current model Colita, at verified pricing Alternative routes to the compound

The argument is substitution, not saving

A London professional buying a premium coffee and a CGA supplement spends roughly $9.25 a day across the two. One Colita serving at $4.57–6.35 replaces both.

That is a stronger position than being cheapest. Cheapest invites a price war with commodity anaerobic lots. Substitution competes on what the cup contains — which is the only ground where the fermentation work counts.

Read the first bar as a warning

$1.50 per serving is the current model, and it is the same £5.90 per 100 g that lands mid-commodity in the UK retail chart earlier. The gap between the two amber bars is not a price rise — it is what the laboratory work buys.

Until a certificate of analysis exists, only the pale bar is defensible.

Business model

Stop buying coffee. Start commissioning it.

Three revenue lines off one production capability, ordered by how quickly each can reach revenue.

Line 01

Bio-Concierge subscription

Consultation, custom protocol design, laboratory verification, recurring delivery. Target $75–150 per customer per month.

Line 02

B2B white-label

Protocol production for premium London cafés and wellness brands who want a differentiated lot they cannot engineer themselves.

Line 03

Extract licensing

High-concentration CGA extract supplied to functional food and beverage manufacturers. The natural home for ultrasound-assisted extraction.

Already selling

Colita green lots presented at retail with per-lot cards — the same commissioning conversation the Bio-Concierge model formalises, already happening across a counter.

Why London first

The densest specialty market that will pay for chemistry.

  • Specialty density — the UK's deepest concentration of independent roasters and third-wave buyers
  • Proven price tolerance — £21–£43 per 100 g already clears in this market
  • Functional beverage appetite — a consumer base already buying for effect, not only flavour
  • Colombian origin advantage — direct farm access is a genuine and defensible moat

Groundwork already built

A complete UK operating system exists in the unroast-brand-os repository: food business registration, traceability and recall policy, COA requirements, batch release records, claims governance against the GB Nutrition and Health Claims Register, and a London same-day delivery model.

Built for a different product. Directly portable as compliance and operations infrastructure.

The moat is 8,000 km away — and that is the point

A London roaster can buy a fermented lot. It cannot run a fermentation programme at origin. Direct farm access is what makes the protocol reproducible rather than a one-off purchase.

Where we are

This is an operating exporter, not a concept.

Colita already grows, processes, cups, bags and ships differentiated coffee under its own export marks. The missing piece is not the business — it is the instrumental evidence for what the process does to the chemistry.

Read the sacks

Named process lots, already shipping.

Black Honey and Yellow Honey are distinct fermentation and drying regimes, bagged separately under the Café de Colita mark and moving as direct trade. The shipping cartons behind them carry Asian consignee labels.

A producer that cannot control fermentation cannot separate a Black Honey from a Yellow Honey lot. The process control the deck claims is visible on the sacks.
